definitions.definition: Every dharma is empty of own-nature because it arises dependently; emptiness is dependent origination, a dependent designation and the middle way (MMK 24.18); it is not a further entity and is itself empty (13.7–8).
The mere absence of own-nature, a non-implicative negation, in persons and phenomena alike (PsP 24.18; MA 6).
The lack of own-nature shown by the absence of true unity and plurality (MAL 1).

relations.note: MMK 24.18 names emptiness and dependent origination as one
the Madhyamaka systematizes the sūtras' emptiness
Madhyamaka refuses to take emptiness as a positive ground; Advaita's Brahman is a positive reality
the Nāth 'void' is a state or ground to be realized; Madhyamaka's emptiness is the absence of own-nature
elaboration ceases in emptiness (MMK 18.5)

definitions.definition: Own-nature would be unfabricated and independent (MMK 15.1–2); since everything is produced by causes and conditions, nothing has it, and without own-nature there is no other-nature, existence or non-existence (15.3–6).

relations.note: own-nature of dharmas is the Abhidharma notion under examination

definitions.definition: The Buddhas teach relying on two truths, the worldly conventional and the ultimate; without the conventional the ultimate cannot be taught, and without the ultimate nirvāṇa is not reached (MMK 24.8–10).

Each thing has two natures, found by correct and by false seeing (MA 6.23); saṃvṛti is ignorance that covers reality, mutual dependence, or worldly convention (PsP 24.8); reality is beyond the intellect (BCA 9.2).
The conventional divides into correct and incorrect (Jñānagarbha) and is the ladder to the ultimate (Bhāviveka), which divides into nominal and non-nominal.
Conventionally, things are mind-only and satisfy only when unexamined; ultimately even mind lacks own-nature (MAL 64, 92–93).

relations.note: Theravāda's ultimate includes real dhammas; Madhyamaka's ultimate is their emptiness
the Kośa's ultimately existent (paramārthasat) dharmas are what Madhyamaka analyses as empty
under P1-level both distinguish worldly usage from the ultimate; Madhyamaka has no positive substrate and no third 'illusory' level; both traditions reject identity

definitions.definition: Things, the self, the Tathāgata and emptiness itself exist as designations made in dependence on a basis, as a chariot on its parts (MMK 24.18; 22.8; PsP on 24.18).

relations.note: PsP on 24.18

definitions.definition: The path free of the extremes of existence and non-existence, eternalism and annihilationism, identified with emptiness and dependent origination (MMK 24.18; 15.7–10; RĀ 1.61–62).

relations.note: the same middle between 'is' and 'is not'

definitions.definition: Emptiness too is empty: there is nothing non-empty for it to be the emptiness of as an entity (MMK 13.7); 'empty' is only said for designation (22.11); by habituation even the notion 'nothing exists' is abandoned (BCA 9.33).

relations.note: one of the listed emptinesses

definitions.definition: Emptiness is the relinquishing of all views; those for whom emptiness is a view are incurable (MMK 13.8); the Buddha taught for the abandonment of all views (27.30).
Like one who asks for the 'nothing' he was offered, or a medicine that stays in the stomach, emptiness taken as a view cannot cure (PsP on 13.8).

relations.note: guards against reifying emptiness

definitions.definition: Dependent origination is without cessation, arising, annihilation, permanence, unity, plurality, coming and going (MMK dedication).
Nothing arises from itself, from another, from both or without cause (MMK 1.1; 21.13).
Refuted one by one in MA 6.8–104, beginning with arising from self, rejected by Buddhapālita as pointless and endless.

relations.note: Gauḍapāda's non-origination uses the same fourfold negation; the grounds differ (unborn Brahman vs. emptiness)

definitions.definition: Four alternatives — is, is not, both, neither — none of which is asserted of the ultimate (MMK 22.11; 25.17–18); in 18.8 the four statements form the Buddhas' (graded) instruction.

name: The similes of illusion, dream and mirage

definitions.definition: Arising, abiding and ceasing, and afflictions, actions, bodies, agents and fruits are like an illusion, a dream, a city of gandharvas or a mirage (MMK 7.34; 17.33; 23.8); empty words negate like one magical man stopping another (VV 23).
Whatever is held real lacks own-nature, being neither truly one nor truly many, like a reflection (MAL 1); a thing without real unity cannot be a real plurality of such units.

name: The nominal and the non-nominal ultimate

definitions.definition: The ultimate beyond all elaboration (aparyāya) and the ultimate accordant with it — the negation of arising and the wisdom of reasoning (paryāya) (Tarkajvālā on MH 3).
Appearances that function as they appear are the correct conventional; those that do not (a mirage as water) the incorrect (Jñānagarbha); the correct conventional is the ladder to reality (MH 3.12).
Conventional things satisfy only when unexamined, arise and cease, and can function (MAL 64).
Candrakīrti distinguishes the correct and incorrect conventional only from the world's standpoint; for the noble ones all of it is merely conventional (MA 6.25–28, from memory).

name: The Tathāgata sought in five ways

definitions.definition: The Tathāgata is not the aggregates, not other than them, not in them, they are not in him, and he does not possess them; he is a designation, empty as the world is empty (MMK 22.1, 22.8, 22.16).

relations.note: the same fivefold search applied to the Buddha

name: The two chariots: Yogācāra and Madhyamaka

definitions.definition: Relying on mind-only one understands the non-existence of external objects; relying on Madhyamaka one understands that mind too is selfless; riding both with the reins of reasoning one is a true Mahāyānist (MAL 92–93).

relations.note: Candrakīrti rejects mind-only even conventionally

definitions.definition: Candrakīrti expounds the emptinesses of the Perfection of Wisdom — sixteen in detail and four in brief — as the emptiness of persons and phenomena (MA 6.179–223).

Later Indian and Tibetan doxographies divide Mādhyamikas: by method into Prāsaṅgika and Svātantrika; by the account of the conventional into Sautrāntika-Madhyamaka (external objects conventionally, Bhāviveka) and Yogācāra-Madhyamaka (mind-only conventionally, Śāntarakṣita); Maitrīpa's Tattvaratnāvalī into those holding non-duality illusion-like and those holding the non-foundation of all dharmas; the Jñānasārasamuccaya ranks Madhyamaka above the other tenet systems.

name: The self as a dependent designation

definitions.definition: The self is neither the aggregates nor other than them (MMK 18.1), neither the appropriated nor apart from it (27.8), related to them as fire to fuel (10.15); like a plantain tree split apart, the person analysed into elements is nothing (RĀ 2.1).
Like a chariot sought in seven ways, the self is not found yet is designated in dependence on the aggregates (MA 6.151–160).

relations.note: the Upaniṣadic self is a real, unchanging subject; Madhyamaka finds no such self
the Pudgalavādins' person 'neither same as nor different from' the aggregates is inexpressible but real; Madhyamaka holds it a mere designation

name: The fivefold analysis (of self or Tathāgata)

definitions.definition: Sought as identical with the aggregates, different from them, containing them, contained in them, or possessing them, the self (or Tathāgata or person) is not found (MMK 16.2; 22.1).

name: The sevenfold analysis of the chariot

definitions.definition: The chariot is not other than its parts, not identical with them, does not possess them, is not in them, does not contain them, is not their collection and not their shape; so the self and the aggregates (MA 6.151–160).
Selflessness of persons and of dharmas: the Buddhas taught self, no-self and neither (MMK 18.6); the aggregates, dharmas and the Tathāgata are all without own-nature.
Both are realized by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as well as bodhisattvas (Candrakīrti, MAbh on 1.8).
Two related things established neither as one nor as different are not established at all: goer and going (MMK 2.18–21), fire and fuel (10.1), self and aggregates (18.1).
Consciousness is self-illuminating because it is not inert; accepted conventionally (MAL 16–17).
Refuted: mind does not see mind, as a blade does not cut itself (BCA 9.17ff); memory does not prove reflexive awareness (MA 6.72–77).

Action and afflictions come from conceptual construction, which comes from elaboration; elaboration ceases in emptiness (MMK 18.5); the ultimate and nirvāṇa are the pacification of elaboration (18.9; 25.24).

Taking the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the impure as pure and the selfless as self; the afflictions arise in dependence on the errors about pleasant and unpleasant and ignorance ceases with them (MMK 23.1–2, 23.23); Catuḥśataka chs. 1–4 overcome them in turn.

name: Mind and its parts in Madhyamaka

definitions.definition: The Abhidharma analysis of mind — consciousness arising from faculty and object (MMK 3.7), the aggregates, intention (17.2–3), the afflictions (23) — is accepted as conventional description; under analysis the mind is not found as a real entity, and the domain of mind ceases in the nature of things (18.7).
No storehouse consciousness and no reflexive awareness are needed even conventionally; the continuum of the aggregates suffices for karma (MA 6; BCA 9.73).
When analysing wisdom finds no dharma arisen in the three times, the yogin enters non-conceptual wisdom pacifying all elaboration (Bhāvanākrama III).
When neither being nor non-being remains before the mind, it is pacified without object (BCA 9.34–35).
The scriptures' non-recollection and non-attention must be preceded by correct analysis of reality; mere stopping of thought is like fainting and cannot remove the obscurations (Bhāvanākrama III).

name: Meditation as mere absence of thought (as criticized)

definitions.definition: The position that awakening is reached by simply not thinking or attending to anything, criticized by Kamalaśīla as leading only to dullness (Bhāvanākrama III); in the Tibetan accounts ascribed to the Chan master Moheyan at Samye.

notes: Stated from the critic's side; Moheyan's own account is in the Dunhuang sources (see dsp:sudden-or-gradual).

definitions.definition: Insight joined with calm destroys the afflictions, so calm should be sought first (BCA 8.4).
Calm stabilizes the mind; insight arises from analysis; the two are balanced by removing laxity and excitement (Bhāvanākrama).

The body is analysed into its parts and elements and not found as a self (BCA 9.58–60; RĀ 2.1); it is to be protected as an instrument for beings' benefit and given to them (ŚSK 4–5); bodies arise from action and afflictions, which are empty (MMK 17.27). No subtle-body anatomy of channels and centres is taught in these sūtra-path texts (that belongs to the Vajrayāna).
Space and the other five elements are neither existent nor non-existent, neither characterized nor characteristic (MMK 5.7); the person is not the six elements, singly or together (RĀ 2.1).

Dependent origination, free of the eight extremes, is the pacification of elaboration (dedication) and is emptiness (24.18); conventionally the twelve links, by which the ignorant forms the formations and suffering arises, and by whose knowledge it ceases (MMK 26); whoever sees it sees the four truths (24.40).

name: The twelve links in the Madhyamaka

definitions.definition: The twelve links are taught conventionally (MMK 26); they arise from conceiving caused things as real and cease when things are seen as empty (ŚS 64–65); grouped as afflictions, actions and suffering in the Pratītyasamutpādahṛdaya.

Action is intention and intended action (MMK 17.2–3); if it lasted until ripening it would be permanent, if it perished it could bear no fruit (17.6); because it is without own-nature it is unarisen and so does not perish (17.21); agent and action are like emanations (17.31–33).
Agent and enjoyer are spoken of with reference to the unity of a continuum (BCA 9.73); the Mādhyamika does not deny action and fruit but their own-nature (PsP 17.30).

relations.note: the realist 'imperishable' is not needed if action is empty
shared doctrine of action and fruit, but denied own-nature

name: The imperishable (avipraṇāśa) of action

definitions.definition: A realist theory stated in MMK 17.13–20: an imperishable factor, like a debt-note, connects action to its fruit, morally indeterminate and abandoned only by cultivation (17.14–15); Nāgārjuna answers from the emptiness of action (17.21ff).

notes: Commentators ascribe the theory to the Sāṃmitīyas.

definitions.definition: Not abandoned, not attained, neither annihilated nor eternal, neither ceased nor arisen (MMK 25.3); neither existent nor non-existent (25.4–10); what, when grasping and depending, is saṃsāra, is nirvāṇa when not grasping and not depending (25.9); the ending of the conceptions of existence and non-existence (RĀ 1.42).

relations.note: a shared goal-word, but nirvāṇa is not an attained state of an existent self

name: The non-difference of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa

definitions.definition: There is not the least difference between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; their limits are the same (MMK 25.19–20); there is nothing to superimpose on nirvāṇa and nothing to remove from saṃsāra (16.10); those who see reality conceive neither (YṢ 5–6).
Because of great compassion the Buddhas do not abide in nirvāṇa but remain acting for the whole world (Bhāvanākrama I).

The two goods of the Ratnāvalī: first the dharma of higher status (good rebirth through ethics and giving), then definite goodness (liberation through the insight that 'I' and 'mine' are false); faith leads to the first, wisdom to the second (RĀ 1.3–5).

name: Refutation of the Lokāyata denial of rebirth

definitions.definition: Consciousness cannot arise from the body alone; each moment of awareness arises from a prior moment of awareness, so the series continues after death (Tattvasaṅgraha, Lokāyata examination).

name: Death and impermanence in the Madhyamaka manuals

definitions.definition: Recollection that one will die and go alone, leaving relatives and possessions (BCA 2.32, 2.62), and that all born beings are subject to the lord of death (CŚ ch.1), turns the mind from craving toward the Dharma; nirvāṇa and the Tathāgata after death are not described by the four alternatives (MMK 25.17–18).

name: The awakening mind (bodhicitta) in the Madhyamaka manuals

definitions.definition: The resolve for awakening for all beings, born with compassion and non-dual understanding (MA 1.1); an elixir transforming the body (BCA 1.10); aspiring and engaging (BCA 1.15–16); relative and ultimate.
The second of the three points after compassion (Bhāvanākrama I).

relations.note: the treatises systematize the sūtras' teaching

definitions.definition: The awakening mind is twofold, as aspiration and as engagement, like the wish to go and actually going (BCA 1.15–16).

The conventional awakening mind is the compassionate resolve and its practice; the ultimate awakening mind is the direct understanding of emptiness (Bodhicittavivaraṇa; instructions on cultivating the two awakening minds in the Tengyur).

Giving, discipline, patience, vigour, meditation and wisdom, each the subject of a chapter of the Bodhicaryāvatāra (5–9) or a ground of the Madhyamakāvatāra (1–6); all are taught for the sake of wisdom (BCA 9.1).
The six with method, aspiration, power and knowledge, each predominant on one of the ten grounds (MA chs. 1–10).
Since happiness is equally dear and suffering equally unwelcome to self and others, one protects all as oneself, as the many limbs are protected as one body (BCA 8.90–96; ŚSK 1).

relations.note: cultivated first (ādau) in BCA 8.90

definitions.definition: The supreme secret: giving oneself to others and taking others as oneself, since all suffering comes from desiring one's own happiness and all happiness from desiring others' (BCA 8.120–136).
Compassion for beings who cling to 'I' and 'mine'; compassion seeing beings as impermanent; and compassion seeing them as empty of own-nature, like the moon in rippling water (MA 1.3–4).
Compassion is the seed, water and ripening of buddhahood and is praised first (MA 1.2).
Compassion alone is the root of all Buddha qualities and is cultivated first (Bhāvanākrama I).
Neither method without wisdom nor wisdom without method liberates the bodhisattva (Bhāvanākrama II); the Buddha's teaching has emptiness and compassion as its essence (RĀ 4.96).
The collection of merit gives rise to the form bodies and the collection of wisdom to the truth body (RĀ 3.12–13).

name: The ten virtuous paths of action

definitions.definition: Refraining from killing, stealing and sexual misconduct, from false, divisive, harsh and idle speech, and from covetousness, malice and wrong views (RĀ 1.8–9); the foundation of higher status.

relations.note: the same list in the Pali suttas

name: The bodhisattva's training: give, protect, purify, increase

definitions.definition: The training is to give away one's body, enjoyments and merit of the three times to all beings, and to protect, purify and increase them (ŚSK 4), rooted in faith and the resolve for awakening (ŚSK 2).

name: Graded teaching fitted to the hearer

definitions.definition: The Buddhas taught self, no-self and neither (MMK 18.6) and the four statements of 18.8 as graded instruction; like a grammarian teaching the alphabet, the Buddha taught some to avoid evil, some for merit, some based on duality and some the profound non-dual (RĀ 4.94–96); first turn from demerit, then from self, then from all views (CŚ 8.15).

relations.note: the graded teaching grounds the provisional/definitive distinction

name: Provisional and definitive meaning in Madhyamaka

definitions.definition: Teachings of arising, self and mind-only are provisional (neyārtha), requiring interpretation, while teachings of emptiness and non-arising are definitive (nītārtha), following the Akṣayamatinirdeśa (PsP 1; MA 6.94ff).

One impartial, intelligent and eager is a vessel for hearing (CŚ 12.1); one who at the mention of emptiness feels joy, tears and horripilation is a vessel to whom the ultimate should be taught (MA 6.4–5); emptiness wrongly grasped harms the dull, so the Buddha hesitated to teach (MMK 24.11–12).

The tradition's line runs from the Buddha's Perfection of Wisdom through Nāgārjuna (who received the sūtras from the nāgas in the tradition's account), Āryadeva and Rāhulabhadra, to the commentators Buddhapālita, Bhāviveka and Candrakīrti, Śāntideva, and Śrīgupta–Jñānagarbha–Śāntarakṣita–Kamalaśīla, and on to Tibet (Atiśa; Patsab Nyima Drak) and China (Kumārajīva). Commentary on a root text by a lineage master is the mode of transmission; no secret initiation is required, but emptiness is to be taught only to a fit vessel.

name: Fear of emptiness and its end

definitions.definition: 'I am not, I will not be' terrifies the childish and ends fear for the wise (RĀ 1.26); emptiness calms suffering, so if there is no 'I' whose would the fear be? (BCA 9.56–57).

name: The qualities of the bodhisattva grounds

definitions.definition: On attaining the first ground the bodhisattva gains twelve sets of a hundred qualities — seeing a hundred Buddhas, receiving their blessing, living a hundred aeons, entering a hundred concentrations, shaking a hundred worlds and so on — multiplying on the higher grounds (MA ch.11).

notes: List from memory of MA's chapter on the qualities of the grounds; to check.

definitions.definition: An omniscient being is possible: the mind, freed from the afflictions by cultivating selflessness, can know all things; this answers the Mīmāṃsā denial (Tattvasaṅgraha, last examination; MH 10).

Present and future are not established without the past, nor with it; time does not exist apart from existents, and no existent exists by own-nature, so time is not found (MMK 19.3, 19.6); saṃsāra has no beginning or end (11.1).

name: The world and its extent in Madhyamaka

definitions.definition: Saṃsāra is beginningless (MMK 11.1); the views that the world is eternal or not, finite or infinite rest on the prior and posterior ends and do not arise for one who sees all as empty (27.1–2, 27.29); the three realms and the ten virtuous and non-virtuous paths are taught conventionally (RĀ 1).

relations.note: the same set of undetermined questions

definitions.definition: Words are dependently arisen and empty yet function (VV 22–23); 'empty' is said only for designation (MMK 22.11); the ultimate is taught only through convention (24.10); in reality the object to be named has ceased (18.7) and no dharma was taught by the Buddha to anyone (25.24).

relations.note: the Word-brahman is refuted in the Tattvasaṅgraha

definitions.definition: The Abhidharma's four conditions, own-natures of dharmas, conditioned characteristics (arising, abiding, ceasing), the unconditioned and the 'imperishable' of karma are examined and shown not to exist by own-nature (MMK 1, 7, 17).

Arising from itself (the pre-existent effect) is pointless and endless (Buddhapālita on MMK 1.1); primal matter cannot be the one eternal cause of the world (MH 6); the Sāṃkhyas are among those who do not pass beyond 'is' and 'is not' (RĀ 1.61).
The means of knowledge are established neither by themselves nor by others nor by their objects (VV 31–51); the sixteen categories are ground down as mutually dependent (Vaidalyaprakaraṇa).
Bhāviveka's chapter on the Vedānta sets out the doctrine of the one eternal self (puruṣa) and rejects a permanent agentless self as unable to act or be known (MH 8).
Śāntarakṣita rejects the Upaniṣadic single eternal consciousness because cognitions are many and momentary (TS, examination of the self).
The authorless Veda and the denial of an omniscient being are rejected (MH 9–10).
The same in the Tattvasaṅgraha's examinations of revelation and of the seer of supersensible things.

name: Madhyamaka's critique of a creator God

definitions.definition: If Īśvara creates unwillingly he depends on another, if by desire he depends on desire; the elements are not Īśvara (BCA 9.119–126).
An eternal cause would produce all effects at once or never (TS, examination of Īśvara).

Consciousness is no more real than its object; reflexive awareness and the storehouse are rejected; 'mind only' denies a creator other than mind and is of provisional meaning (MA 6.45–97; BCA 9.15–25).
Bhāviveka rejects the real other-dependent nature and accepts external objects conventionally (MH 5).
The Mādhyamika must state formal inferences with reason and example, qualified 'ultimately' (Bhāviveka, PP 1).
Not appropriate for one who has no position of his own (PsP 1).
Refuting by drawing out the unwanted consequences of the opponent's own theses, as Buddhapālita did on MMK 1.1, defended by Candrakīrti (PsP 1).

The Mādhyamika has no thesis of his own, so the faults of a thesis do not apply (VV 29); one without a position of existence, non-existence or both cannot be refuted (CŚ 16.25); the great-souled have no position (YṢ 50).
